sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: 'the seal is the water'
sections.b: In the Shepherd of Hermas, a Roman book of the second century in no church's Bible, baptism is 'the seal'. The Shepherd explains that before a person bears the name of the Son of God he is dead: 'But when he receives the seal, he lays aside his deadness and takes up life' (Shepherd of Hermas 93:3). 'So the seal is the water. They go down into the water dead, and they come up alive' (Shepherd of Hermas 93:4). No one, even the righteous who died before Christ, can enter the kingdom of God without it (Shepherd of Hermas 93:2), and the nations of the world become one body by receiving it (Shepherd of Hermas 94:4). The language echoes John 3:5 and Romans 6:3-4, and 2 Clement uses 'the seal' the same way (2 Clement 7:6; 8:6).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 93:2-4; Shepherd of Hermas 94:4; John 3:5; Romans 6:3-4; 2 Clement 7:6; 2 Clement 8:6

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the dead baptized by the apostles
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas (Rome, second century) pictures the apostles and teachers, after their own deaths, preaching to the righteous who had died before them and giving them 'the seal of the preaching': 'they went down into the water with them and came up again' (Shepherd of Hermas 93:5-6). In Hermas the dead receive baptism themselves. What Paul's baptism 'for the dead' (1 Corinthians 15:29) was is disputed; the card at that verse sets out the readings, and Hermas does not cite it. Clement of Alexandria quotes the passage twice (Stromata 2.9; 6.6).

uncommon: The Shepherd of Hermas has the righteous dead baptized by apostles who had died, in the world of the dead (Shepherd of Hermas 93:5-6).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: apostles preach to the dead
sections.b: In the Shepherd of Hermas it is not Christ but 'these apostles and teachers, who preached the name of the Son of God', who after falling asleep 'preached to those who had fallen asleep before them as well' (Shepherd of Hermas 93:5). Lake's note on the verse compares 1 Peter 3:19, the Gospel of Peter (where a voice from heaven says, 'You have preached to them that sleep') and the descent in the Acts of Pilate, and comments that 'it is more usually the Christ himself who descends to Hades for the purpose'. Hermas never names Hades.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 93:5-7; 1 Peter 3:19; 1 Peter 4:6; Gospel of Peter 10

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: twelve tribes, twelve nations
sections.b: In the great parable of the tower in the Shepherd of Hermas, the twelve mountains are 'the tribes that live in the whole world', and the Shepherd explains at once that they are 'twelve nations', to whom 'The Son of God was preached to them through the apostles' (Shepherd of Hermas 94:1-2). The twelve tribes of Israel have become the peoples of the earth gathered into one church, as in James 1:1 ('the twelve tribes in the Dispersion') on one reading.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: deacons who robbed widows
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas condemns 'deacons who served badly', who 'robbed widows and orphans of their living, and... made gain for themselves from the ministry they had been given'. They are dead unless they turn back and 'complete their ministry in purity' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:2). The passage shows deacons in the Roman church handling the care of widows and orphans, as the Seven did in Acts 6:1-6, and the temptation 1 Timothy 3:8 warns against.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the hospitable overseers
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas praises 'overseers and people who welcome guests', who took God's slaves into their homes and 'by their ministry, always sheltered those in need and the widows' (Shepherd of Hermas 104:2). The overseers are plural. Elsewhere the book names apostles, overseers, teachers and deacons together (Shepherd of Hermas 13:1) and the elders who lead the church in Rome (Shepherd of Hermas 8:3), without saying how the offices relate. Hospitality is a mark of the overseer in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:8.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 104:2-3; Shepherd of Hermas 13:1; Shepherd of Hermas 8:3; 1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:8

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: overseers who opened their homes
sections.b: The tenth mountain of the Shepherd of Hermas, with trees sheltering sheep, stands for overseers and hospitable believers 'who were always glad to take God's slaves into their homes, without pretending' (Shepherd of Hermas 104:2). The Lord will shelter them forever, and 'their place is already with the angels' (Shepherd of Hermas 104:3).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: widows robbed and sheltered
sections.b: Two chapters of the Shepherd of Hermas set the widows of the Roman church between the bad and the good officers: deacons who 'robbed widows and orphans of their living' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:2), and overseers who 'always sheltered those in need and the widows without fail' (Shepherd of Hermas 104:2). Compare James 1:27 and Mark 12:40.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 103:2; Shepherd of Hermas 104:2; James 1:27; Mark 12:40

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: those who suffered for the name
sections.b: The eleventh mountain of the Shepherd of Hermas is those 'who suffered for the name of the Son of God... and they handed over their lives' (Shepherd of Hermas 105:2; compare Acts 15:26). 'the sins of all of them have been taken away' (Shepherd of Hermas 105:3). Those who did not deny when 'brought before the authorities and questioned' have the better fruit; those who wavered and then suffered, the lesser (Shepherd of Hermas 105:4). Hermas never uses the word martyr; he speaks of suffering for the name.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 105:1-8; Acts 15:26; 1 Peter 4:13-16; Matthew 5:11-12

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the thistles and the round stones
sections.b: In Similitude 9 of the Shepherd of Hermas the rich appear twice. They are the thistles of the third mountain, who keep away from God's slaves 'because they are afraid they will be asked for something' and will enter the kingdom 'only with difficulty' (Shepherd of Hermas 97:1-3; compare Matthew 19:23). They are also the round stones from the white mountain: their riches 'darkened them a little and dimmed them from the truth', so the Lord had their wealth 'cut back, but not taken from them completely, so that they could do some good with what was left to them' (Shepherd of Hermas 107:4-5; Latin). Vision 3 tells the same picture more sharply (Shepherd of Hermas 14:5-6).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 97:1-4; Shepherd of Hermas 107:4-5; Shepherd of Hermas 108:1-2; Shepherd of Hermas 14:5-6; Matthew 19:23; 1 Timothy 6:17-19

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: slander and poisoned words
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas pictures slanderers as cracks in the stones of a mountain, small ones that can be quickly repented of and large ones that have hardened into grudges (Shepherd of Hermas 100:2-3), and as the snakes of a desert mountain: 'just as the beasts destroy a person with their poison and kill him, so the words of people like this destroy a person and kill him' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:7; compare James 3:8).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 100:1-5; Shepherd of Hermas 103:7-8; James 3:8; James 4:11

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: repentance before the tower is finished
sections.b: The explanation of the twelve mountains in the Shepherd of Hermas offers repentance to almost every kind of believer, usually on condition that it be quick, and refuses it only to apostates and betrayers (Shepherd of Hermas 96:1). For those who denied their Lord 'long ago, repentance seems to be there', but not for anyone who plans to deny now, and it must come 'before the tower is finished' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:5-6). The book's last words return to it: the building has been paused for the hearers' sake, and 'unless you hurry to do right, the tower will be finished, and you will be shut out' (Shepherd of Hermas 114:4; Latin). Those who repented with all their hearts have their sins smoothed over like marks filled in a wall (Shepherd of Hermas 110:3).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 96:1-3; Shepherd of Hermas 103:5-6; Shepherd of Hermas 110:3; Shepherd of Hermas 114:4; Hebrews 6:4-6; 2 Peter 3:9

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: denial from the heart
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas separates those who denied their Lord under pressure from those 'found to have denied from the heart': for the first there is repentance; of the second the Shepherd says, 'I do not know if he can live' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:5). For anyone who is 'going to deny his Lord now', it is 'impossible... to be saved' (Shepherd of Hermas 103:6), language close to Hebrews 6:4-6.

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: death brought on by despair
sections.b: In the last chapter of the Shepherd of Hermas (Latin only), the angel says that the poor suffer like people in chains, and that 'many people, because of disasters like these, bring death on themselves when they cannot bear them'. The Latin does not say how; it may mean taking one's own life, or dying through despair. He does not judge the act; he blames those who could help: whoever knows of such distress 'and does not rescue him commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood' (Shepherd of Hermas 114:3).

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: woe to the shepherds
sections.b: Near the end of the Shepherd of Hermas the angel of repentance warns the church's leaders: if any sheep are found to have fallen away, 'it will be woe to the shepherds', and if the shepherds themselves fall away they cannot blame the sheep, 'For it is unbelievable that a shepherd should suffer harm from sheep'. The Shepherd adds that he too must 'give a very strict account' (Shepherd of Hermas 108:5-6), as Hebrews 13:17 says of leaders and Ezekiel 34 of Israel's shepherds.
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 108:4-6; Ezekiel 34:1-10; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:2-4

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: one body from twelve mountains
sections.b: In Similitude 9 of the Shepherd of Hermas the stones of twelve different mountains turn one bright color in the tower, because the nations 'received the seal' and 'had one insight and one mind. Their faith became one and their love one' (Shepherd of Hermas 94:4; compare Ephesians 4:4-6). The church on earth is mixed; when the evil, the hypocrites and the double-minded are thrown out, 'the church of God will be one body, one insight, one mind, one faith, one love' (Shepherd of Hermas 95:3-4).
sections.refs: Shepherd of Hermas 94:3-5; Shepherd of Hermas 95:2-4; Ephesians 4:4-6; Ephesians 5:27

sections.h: The Shepherd of Hermas: the neglected vine
sections.b: The Shepherd of Hermas compares believers who have denied and keep away from the church to 'a vine left inside some fence and neglected': the weeds take it, it grows wild, and it is no longer useful to its owner (Shepherd of Hermas 103:4). Compare the lazy man's vineyard in Proverbs 24:30-31.
